doc.title: Anne Phillips interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, February 24, 2025

title: First hearing jazz: Ron Kalina's vocal group and Oberlin
summary: A signed autograph trip led to singing in Ron Kalina's group, hearing Dizzy Gillespie, then Oberlin big band and radio show.

bands.name: Spike Jones and His City Slickers

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: There’s a phrase that I recall from music school and the group of us who wanted to “make it” in the music business.

And at the time I’m not sure we even had a notion of what that was. Some of us wanted — you know like I wanted to play with Blood, Sweat & Tears or that kind of thing. And do you recall at that time setting goals? And what did “make it” mean for you?

No. I’ll tell you where I first heard jazz and this is kind of interesting. My sister, two years younger, was a fine artist and she could draw. And so Wyomissing is outside of Reading, PA. So whoever was coming into town in Reading she would do a portrait of, and then she would go and get it signed. Anyway I happened to love Doodles Weaver. Do you remember Doodles Weaver?
No. Doodles Weaver was the singer with Spike Jones. [sings] Oh “Beetle Bomb”? — and so forth, and “Horse Race” and so forth.

Yes exactly. Well I didn’t know anything about jazz but I knew there had to be something more than Dixieland because I heard people talking about it in high school. But anyway, so I took my sister out to get Doodles’ signed. And it was in this lovely country hotel and there was a guy playing piano who was a local piano player, and so they were very nice to us little girls and he signed his picture. And he said, “What do you want to do when you grow up?” I said well singing. He said, “Well sing something.” So I did. Well the next thing I know I got a call from a guy, Ron Kalina who lived in Reading and had a five voice vocal group and was looking for a girl to sing second. And so, as a senior in high school that was when I realized where I belonged because twice a week I would drive into his row house in Reading and do these hip arrangements. Did you ever hear of the Skylarks?

George — oh no, I can’t quite remember his name — was one of the Skylarks, and he was from Reading. And Ronny wrote those kinds of hip arrangements. And so there I was every Thursday and Sunday singing with real musicians, real jazz musicians. And that was the first time I heard a Dizzy Gillespie record. “Dizzy Atmosphere.” And that’s when I discovered jazz. And Ron kept on going, he was a great harmonica player as well, lived in L.A. and we kept in touch somehow, in a funny way, after years after that. But that was really the start. And then I went to Oberlin and I went in the college, nobody was guiding me. But I auditioned for the big band and I got that, and then I got a weekly radio show.
